title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 319: The Metaphorical Machine
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 319 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

The Metaphorical Machine: Embodied Cognition and Language

Paragraph 1. For decades, cognitive scientists viewed the human mind as a biological computer. Spread by early artificial intelligence researchers and formal linguists, this computational model claimed that thinking simply meant arranging abstract symbols according to mathematical rules. Under this view, our physical senses and bodies were treated as minor outside hardware, while real thinking worked completely independently of flesh, muscles, and movement. In The Flesh of Thought, linguists Dr. Arthur Pence and Dr. Miriam Cho challenge this traditional view.

Paragraph 2. Pence and Cho argue for 'embodied cognition'—the idea that abstract thought grows directly from physical interactions with the world around us. The bridge linking physical life to abstract reasoning is metaphor. Far from being a poetic decoration used only by writers, metaphor acts as the basic operating system of everyday thinking. We understand time through physical motion in space: the future lies 'in front of us', the past stays 'behind us', and deadlines 'approach'. Similarly, we describe affection via temperature ('warm' welcome vs 'cold' stare) and career rank via height (climbing the 'corporate ladder').

Paragraph 3. Modern brain imaging confirms that these everyday metaphors are wired into our biology. When volunteers read phrases like 'she had a rough day' or 'he grasped the idea', fMRI scans show that brain regions linked to physical movement and touch light up—specifically the somatosensory cortex (which senses physical texture) and the motor cortex (which controls hand grasping). The brain literally understands abstract ideas by reactivating circuits originally built for physical action.

Paragraph 4. Finally, Pence and Cho explain what this means for artificial intelligence. Silicon computer chips lack living flesh, touch, and physical mortality; although they process symbols at astonishing speed, they cannot genuinely understand what words mean. An algorithm has never felt the warmth of an embrace or the heaviness of exhaustion. Until machines possess a physical body that interacts directly with the material world, true understanding will remain uniquely human.
